newsitem.title: UK: DOLLAR STEADY AS STERLING TAKES CENTRE STAGE.
newsitem.headline: DOLLAR STEADY AS STERLING TAKES CENTRE STAGE.

text.p: The dollar took a back seat to sterling in midsession Europe as concern that UK interest rates have peaked overshadowed news of a rate rise and triggered a slump in the pound.
The Bank of England raised UK rates to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent at the end of its two-day meeting but said rates were now at levels consistent with the government's inflation targets.
Traders viewed this as a signal that UK rates will not rise further and dumped pounds. Sterling suffered equally against the dollar and the mark, leaving dollar/mark little affected.
"Sterling is back below the psychological three-mark level because the Bank (of England) has signalled that rates are on hold for now," said Nick Stamencovic, economist at DKB International.
"But the pound has more downside potential against the dollar than the mark given that the U.S. fundamentals are so much better," he said.
Sterling/mark was at 2.9980/90 at 1130 GMT, down from 3.0130 late in Europe on Wednesday while cable fell to $1.5960/70 from $1.6038 on Wednesday.
Dollar/mark was at 1.8792/97 from 1.8808 late on Wednesday. The U.S. currency was at 118.59/69 yen from 118.53 on Wednesday.

But traders are expected to switch their focus back to dollar/mark soon. Speculation is rife the Bundesbank will allow money-market rates to drift higher if the mark slides beyond the near-eight-year low it has been lingering at against the dollar.

That speculation helped the U.S. currency pare some of its gains. But dollar bulls are raring to push the dollar higher on expectations Germany's economic recovery is not robust enough to withstand significantly higher rates.
"The markets are pushing the dollar higher because they realise that whatever Germany does, it cannot be too aggressive," said Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London.
This and evidence the U.S. economy is expanding at a healthy pace without stoking inflation is prompting traders to look for the dollar to climb to new peaks in the coming days.

"The market has a 1.90 target in mind and if it has a target, it will go there," said James McKay, economist at PaineWebber. "The dollar has pushed up to these highs on relatively little news so it needs little new incentive to get there."
But the dollar is expected to struggle to gain strongly against the yen, given persistent concern about the potential for trade tensions between the U.S. and Japan.

Comments made by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky on Wednesday fanned such concern and triggered demand for yen in Asia. She said Japan should not rely too much on exports to promote growth and that she was disappointed by the recent drop in U.S. automotive sales to Japan.
This drove dollar/yen down from yesterday's 12-week's highs and pushed the mark down to 62.75 yen, the weakest it has been since July 1995.
Traders expect more such comments and a barrage of verbal intervention from Japanese officials if the dollar attempts to climb back above 120 yen.
"Trade tensions are continuing to weigh on dollar/yen and more U.S. comments will cap the upside," said Stamencovic at DKB.
